Title: Ep. 78, Equity by Design: How Diversity Ignites Creativity
Video URL: https://youtu.be/39-kYM48a0Q
Categories: BUSINESS
Transcript:
[MUSIC] There is one catalyst that can amplify your organization's creativity and ignite its impact. Today, we will talk about the importance and value of diversity in our social networks. I'm Matt Abrahams, and I teach strategic communication at Stanford Graduate School of Business. Welcome to Think Fast, Talk Smart, The Podcast. [MUSIC] Today I am super excited to be joined by Adina Sterling, who is an associate professor of organizational behavior at Stanford GSB. Adina studies the causes and consequences of human relationships in organizations and markets. And she teaches a popular elective class called Equity by Design, and runs a lab by the same name. Welcome Adina, I'm super excited to get a chance to talk with you. >> Thanks, Matt, it's great to be here. >> Yes, well, thanks for being here. So let's go ahead and get started. A lot of your work focuses on social networks. For many of us, social networks refer to applications like Facebook, or Twitter, and LinkedIn. What do you mean by social networks and what types of insights can you learn from them? >> Right, so that's a great question to begin with. And you're absolutely right, we hear social networks and we think about Facebook, and LinkedIn, and Instagram, and things that 12 and 13 year olds are more savvy at, than we are. >> Yeah. >> So, what they are, are the patterns of interactions and communication that happens between various entities. So social scientists will study social networks that occur between individuals, between groups, between teams, between societies, organizations, institutions. And so social networks is a construct that travels different levels, and levels of analyses. And we care about them because a lot of the outcomes that individuals, groups, and organizations experience, have to do with the social networks that they have, where they are within this pattern of relationships. And so oftentimes we get a lot of our social resources from social networks, and so they can be awfully important. >> I see, so a social network is essentially a way of mapping the different connections and relationships we have within groupings of people. >> That's right. >> As you know, Adina, this podcast focuses a lot on communication. So I'm wondering, what role does communication play within social networks? And have you been able to determine any best practices that organizations use to maximize the impact of communication within their networks? So communication in the social networks are foundational to why social networks exist. So if I can't communicate effectively to you or you to me, our social tie goes away. So a lot of the way that we understand social ties is the transfer of information, advice, care, social support, and of course being able to communicate those aspects of life effectively. So the care that somebody would express to another depends on their ability to communicate that in a way that's empathetic and real. And so communication is foundational to social networks. What can organizations do to help employees communicate and help employees communicate with clients and other stakeholders? I always hear, Matt, go back to the importance of culture. So if the organization can put into place the right norms, the right expectations, the right language so that people can communicate, and they sort of know where the boundaries are, and where not to cross boundaries. Those can be really helpful ways of helping employees communicate their wants and needs, their ideas to one another and to other stakeholders. >> Wow, so I just learned that I've been a social networking- >> You have. >> Researcher for all these years, and I didn't know that that's what I was. No, that's great. So, thank you for sharing that the communication is absolutely critical in understanding social networks. And it sounds like organizations that put a priority on helping people communicate, the value of communication, and allowing people to feel that notion we've talked about before on this podcast of psychological safety, to feel comfortable communicating- >> That's right. >> Can be much more effective. >> Do you mind if I add one there? >> Please, yeah. >> Piece to what organizations can do, what you just teed up made me think of this. Another important part of communication that organizations can tap into is the notion that it can be multifaceted. So verbal communication, of course, is one way of communicating, auditory communication, but it's not the only way. And so, especially organizations that recognize neurodiversity, for example, will do things in a team setting like take pauses, give people think time. Allow people to write down ideas in the middle of a meeting, so that people's natural strengths, because we all have different strengths, don't all dominate, so that only certain people don't get to communicate their ideas. Organizations that do this well, collect ideas from many different people and allow for communication to come through many different mediums. >> I love that idea and it brings us really nicely into my next set of questions around what you teach in your Equity by Design class, and in the lab that you run. So it's really important from what I'm hearing you say that organizations don't just lock into one way of communicating, that they be very open to multiple ways, and they put a priority on communication. I will often recommend that organizations take time to reflect on their communication at the end of meetings, or one-on-one interaction, spend a few minutes just talking about the quality of the communication, not rehashing what was said, necessarily. And also as part of performance reviews and other big meetings, talk about communication and what you add so nicely to it is, it's not just one monolithic thing, there are lots of different ways to communicate. And we want to make sure that everybody can bring their best selves to the communication. Can you share with us some of the concepts you teach in your Equity by Design class, as well as the topics you study in your Equity by Design lab, what role does communication play in these efforts? >> Sure, so my class, as you mentioned, is on diversity, equity, and inclusion. And those are really three different ideas. In thinking about the importance of communication, it is awfully important for diversity. So let me say a little more about this. >> Please. >> We've now had several decades of work done by social scientists on what diversity buys you, what is the diversity bonus? Has been the question. And when people from different backgrounds that have different ideas come together, what research has shown is that they tend to outperform from a creativity and innovation standpoint, groups that are more homogeneous. But the key to having those benefits come about, is the ability for people to be able to communicate. So you could have a really diverse group- >> Right. >> And if everybody shuts down and nobody's communicating, it becomes really hard to build off of each other's ideas, to have those creative breakthroughs. You need people to be willing to share their thoughts and their ideas. And so that's one way communication is really key. >> The importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion are critical for many aspects of an organization for sure, and I'm curious to hear even more. But in terms of communication, they drive creativity and innovation. And it seems, to me, that it's so important for organizations to Recognize that and celebrate it and to encourage it. Have you seen best practices, or do you teach best practices to really help leaders amplify the diversity that they have, so they can get those results that they're looking for? >> Mm-hm, yeah, so for my class man I have what they call a better practices playbook, so- >> So I love it. So, first before we go, why better practices and not best practices? >> Okay, so that is a good question. The reason is that when it comes to this topic, what I found is that sometimes the great can be the enemy of the good. And so when I first began teaching this topic at Stanford, I had people say to me, my gosh, one of the things I'd like about your class is that we're taught to incrementally, just get going, right? We don't have to have the perfect plan for diversity, equity, and inclusion. What we can do is begin and have better practices from where we're at. So anyway, it's the idea of that the great shouldn't be the enemy of the good. >> I love it. I'm calling them better practices. >> Better practices, that's right. >> All right, what are some from your class? >> Yeah, so one important one is to understand that because diversity has benefits, sometimes you need to do things differently as a leader. The thing that diversity really helps you with is sometimes slowing down to take the time to be creative, to make better choices and have better solutions. So, there was this terrific study done that was actually looking at juries. And they found, these researchers, that juries that were more do diverse, they were more deliberate. People came more prepared and better able to argue their ideas, and outcomes generally reviewed as being better when there are these more diverse groups. And so the first, really it's about buying in [LAUGH] and understanding that it might take a little bit longer to build a diverse team, but that has some benefits in the long run. >> So taking the time and being thoughtful about putting the team together and then giving the team space to actually leverage the diverse perspectives that they bring can be really helpful. >> That's right, that's right. >> A lot of business is so much about rushing and being first and fast. >> That's right. >> And it sounds like what I'm hearing you say is sometimes being more deliberate and slowing down can give you an advantage as well. >> Yes. >> Great. >> Yeah, and then also building up the right culture around the team becomes key. >> Right, so that helping people feel connected and safe and that their voice has value. >> Exactly. >> Yeah, great, many of those listening into our podcast today worked for organizations that are in various stages of implementing their DE&I programs, based on your experience what are some of the best ways to implement, assess, and reinforce these programs? >> Sure, so I'd like to say if you can get by in from the top oftentimes there are grassroots efforts within organizations that are terrific around DEI and leadership can feel as though they're responding to DEI efforts. And that's fine, but if there can be leadership from the top and a collaboration with employees on what their DEI needs and B needs are, that can be a really effective way to go about things. The other concept I would just add here is that I do like to talk about within organizations, what do you think of as. So we all think about innovation and going to be at the bleeding edge. The analogy doesn't quite work the same way. But traditionally, there are more marginalized groups within organizations. And so sometimes, sitting with and taking the temperature of those groups and figuring out how to implement policy changes that are affected there, can have enormous spillover effects for everyone. So, for example, if an organization goes on and surveys all recent parents for mothers, fathers, and the like about time off policies. They'll hear a lot of things in there that could also help older individuals that are taking care of their parents, Individuals that have family that are further away. And so organizations, that sit and listen to more marginalized groups, often times can use those insights, and blow them out and, and have effective policies for multiple groups within organizations. >> That's really, really fantastic. It's starts with listening, and then collaboration, and it has to come, not just from the grassroots, but also from the top and, and that's what leads to success. More and more as I do these podcasts, the role of listening, and taking the time to hear what others are saying is really a key ingredient to success in many aspects. And it sounds like DE&I is no different. I wanted to address another area of your research that I found really fascinating. You've identified something you term the confidence gap as a potential contributor to gender differences we see in the workplace, such as equity and pay. Can you explain what the confidence gap is, and how can it be addressed? >> Sure, so I'm glad we're chatting about this because sometimes the confidence gap can be misunderstood. So, I'll first explain it and then talk about where it comes from because that's a real key to this. So, the confidence gap, that idea came from a study that I and some researchers here at Stanford did where we tracked the outcomes of college students in engineering programs at 27 institutions. And it was a longitudinal study, so we were interested in people's, what we called self-efficacy, how much confidence they had in their ability to do engineering and stem and mathematics type problems early on, how that changed over time, where they were with respect to self-efficacy as they were entering the workplace, and then what happened after they entered. And what we found is that women and men did differ in the level of self-efficacy they felt, or they reported. Okay, so this is a self-perceived measure, if you will, of your own confidence in your ability to solve engineering problems, so on and so forth. So, we did find a gender gap. We found that men had higher levels of confidence than women. We found that this effect held within specific kinds of engineering programs. And so, engineers, I was an engineer as an undergrad Graduate at Ohio State, so there's a lot of engineering snobbery, so sometimes it's like. Well, the aerospace engineers are this smart, and the electrical are this smart, and the chemical or this smart. So, anyway, we wanted to look within engineering major, and we still found this effect. So, it wasn't that women were only going into some engineering fields and men others, and that was leading to this difference in the confidence gap. It remained within engineering nature. It also remained when we looked within GPAs. So when we looked at only those with sort of 3.9 GPA or above which believe it or not, the number of students in our study had that GPA. It remained there. It remained within every GPA category. And so, one of the things we then did, Matt, was say, okay, does this help explain the gender wage gap? And we found the that it did. We did a mediation analysis on the first salaries that people received, and it did. That turned out that once we accounted for the level of self-confidence people had, most of that gender gap could be explained away, now. The thing I want to emphasize, though, is that this gap doesn't come from the sky [LAUGH]. >> Right. >> It comes from our society that provides expectations and norms about who can be an engineer, who should be confident in their ability to be an engineer. So I want to be really careful that this is not about blaming- >> Right. >> Women, that they're less confident. This is coming from a society that conditioned women in different ways from men to be confident in their abilities. And so one of the things that sometimes I'll get asked is, okay, well what can we do about this? >> Right. >> And I'm really quick to say, okay, this is not a fix the women- >> Right, right. >> kind of thing. There's lots of things that we can do, especially within STEM where our study focused. We know that when you diversify the faculty, and you have more female faculty that can have important signaling value for women and increase their confidence. You can structure teams in ways that there's greater gender balance. And so something that can happen in engineering, and this doesn't necessarily reflect my experience, but some research and also anecdotes, I'll share that. In engineering programs, you'll have five-person teams, sometimes one woman, and then that one woman is the note taker. So there's all sorts of small, daily kinds of interactions and ways of communicating within groups that can lead people to have different levels of confidence in their abilities. And we just need to figure out ways to stop all of this. >> There's been an underlying theme in our conversation today, Adina, around the impact of the culture and the norms within organizations, or in the case of what we just discussed, society. And what I'm taking away, and I'd love for you to verify this is that, to make the kind of change that you're talking about, we've talked about in other episodes here, it's really about looking at the larger factors that are influencing the communication or behavior. And that's where you have to adjust, and adapt, and focus, to have the kind of impact that we're talking about. >> Mm-hm. >> And while that can feel daunting, I think you've got some evidence, and I know in what you teach, some better practices for how to go about doing that, so thank you. Before we end, I'd like to ask you the same three questions I ask everyone who joins me. Does that sound all right? >> That sounds great. >> All right, if you were to capture the best communication advice you have ever received as a five to seven word presentation slide title, what would it be? >> What a question. What came to mind for me is, paint a picture, tell a story. >> I love it, paint a picture, tell a story. So we've talked a lot about storytelling here, but give me some more detail about painting a picture, I like it. >> Sure, so when people are hearing your story that you're communicating, if they can put themselves in your shoes or your sets of experiences, that's the picture I'm talking about. And I do think so much of DEI comes from perspective taking, and empathy for those that might be different from us. And so that ability to say, here's how I felt in this moment, and why that can be, I think, an effective way of communicating. >> So true, and as a communicator, if you're looking to paint that picture so people can understand your perspective, it changes your focus. It changes what you're going to say and how you say it. It's going to be about emotion, it's going to be about detail, and that's so critical. And I think when we reflect on the speakers that move us the most, are ones that can do that well. Which leads me nicely, I think, to our second question which is, who is a communicator that you admire, and why? >> All right, so I'm going to not directly answer this question. >> Okay, that's all right. >> But to answer it in the way that this came to me, which is, I grew up going to church, I grew up going to black churches. >> Mm-hm. >> And within that tradition, there are wonderful orators with just really rich linguistic styles. And so, I thought about a number of black politicians today, from that tradition. So Stacey Abrams, Raphael Warnock, Barack Obama. >> Right. >> I could name others, you could name others. There also was a very rich oral tradition because during various parts of history, when black people weren't allowed to be able to read and write. >> Mm-hm. >> What you understood, came from the black church on a Sunday Morning. So, anyway, I really admire that linguistic style and that way of communicating. >> Yeah, well, thank you for sharing, and thank you for taking a very different perspective on that. When I think of the orations I've seen in black churches, the emotion and the ability to move those in the pews is fantastic. And while that style is very appropriate in that moment, many of the aspects of what makes it effective apply in other types of communication, as well. So I appreciate you highlighting that. Third and final question, what are the first three ingredients that go into a successful communication recipe? >> Sure, okay, so, the first is, think about your audience. Think about your audience's perspective, and I feel privileged to be able to practice this as an instructor, as a professor. >> Right. >> And for me, that was a big shift that I made in my teaching trajectory, when I stopped trying to teach, and I started trying to communicate. I thought about those two things differently. And, in fact, I think that communication is just king from that standpoint. The second one is, use emotion rather than shy away from it. >> Okay, yeah, lean in. >> I think lean in is fine, that can be effective. And then, less is more, is my third one. >> So it does not surprise me at all that audience is something that you would absolutely see as important. And that distinction between teaching and communicating, I think all people who are really good instructors have that moment where they realize it's not just about relaying information, it's about connecting. >> Mm-hm. >> Emotion is critical. I think your other answers have highlighted that. It takes a confidence to be able to come to that place, to go in with, I've just got a couple ideas, not all of these ideas- >> Mm-hm. >> And I appreciate that. Well, Adina, thank you. This has been- >> You're welcome. >> Really really insightful, and a lot of fun, and really helpful. Thank you for taking the time for making us better, and for sharing your better practices with us. >> You're welcome, that was a lot of fun. >> Great, you've been listening to an episode of Think Fast, Talk Smart, The Podcast, a production of Stanford Graduate School of Business. This podcast was produced by Jenny Luna, Kevin Patel, and me, Matt Abrahams, with special thanks to Podium Podcast Company. To find more episodes, visit our website@gsb.stanford.edu, or find us wherever you get your podcasts, including YouTube. For more business-related content, follow the Business School on social media at Stanford GSB. You can also find the podcast and follow us on LinkedIn and Instagram. [MUSIC]

# ***Ep. 78, Equity by Design: How Diversity Ignites Creativity***

## What are Social Networks? 
- Social networks refer to patterns of interactions and communication that occur between various entities
- These entities can be individuals, groups, teams, societies, organizations, and institutions
- Social networks exist at different levels and can be analyzed to understand the outcomes that individuals, groups, and organizations experience
- Social networks are important because individuals and groups get a lot of their social resources from these networks

## Importance of Communication in Social Networks 
- Communication is foundational to why social networks exist
- Communication is essential for the transfer of information, advice, care, social support, and ideas
- Communication is critical to understanding social ties and maintaining social relationships
- Organizations that prioritize communication help employees communicate effectively with one another and other stakeholders

## Multifaceted Communication 
- Verbal communication is one way of communicating
- Communication can also occur through different mediums, such as writing or visual aids
- Organizations that recognize neurodiversity can allow communication through many different mediums
- Some organizations take pauses or give people think time, allowing everyone's ideas to be heard

## Equity by Design 
- Diversity, equity, and inclusion are three different ideas that are important to understand
- Diversity bonuses occur when groups with different backgrounds and ideas come together and outperform more homogeneous groups
- Communication is essential for diversity bonuses to occur
- Equity by Design is a class that teaches diversity, equity, and inclusion
- Equity by Design Lab studies the causes and consequences of human relationships in organizations and markets
- Communication is essential for diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts to be successful.
## Importance of Communication and Diversity 

- Communication is key to the success of any organization.
- Diversity, equity, and inclusion are critical for the success of an organization.
- Celebrating diversity and encouraging it can drive creativity and innovation.

## Best Practices for Amplifying Diversity 

- A "Better Practices Playbook" can be used to amplify diversity.
- The playbook emphasizes that organizations don't have to have a perfect plan for diversity, equity, and inclusion.
- The goal is to start and have better practices from where the organization is at.
- Diversity helps to slow down to make better choices and have better solutions.
- Deliberating and taking the time to build a diverse team can have benefits in the long run.
- Building the right culture around the team is also important.

## Implementing, Assessing, and Reinforcing DEI Programs 

- Getting buy-in from leadership is essential.
- Collaboration with employees on their DEI needs is necessary.
- Education is a critical component.
- Listening to marginalized groups can lead to effective policies that benefit everyone.

## The Confidence Gap 

- A study at Stanford tracked self-efficacy, or the confidence in one's ability to do engineering and STEM Mathematics problems.
- Women had lower levels of self-efficacy than men.
- The gap held within specific kinds of engineering programs.
- The confidence gap can be misunderstood.
- Addressing the gap requires understanding its causes.
## Studying the Confidence Gap in Engineering 

- Research focused on the Confidence Gap in engineering among women.
- The study found that women's self-confidence in engineering subject matter was lower than men's.
- However, the results showed that women's self-confidence was not related to their GPAs or engineering field.
  
## The Role of Society in the Confidence Gap 

- The Confidence Gap is not a result of women's lack of confidence, but instead is a product of societal expectations and norms.
- Women are conditioned differently than men to be confident in their abilities to become engineers.
  
## Explaining the Gender Wage Gap 

- The researchers conducted a mediation analysis on the first salaries that people received.
- The analysis found that once the level of self-confidence was accounted for, most of the gender gap in pay could be explained away.
  
## How to Address the Confidence Gap 

- It's not about fixing women but instead looking at larger factors that are influencing communication or behavior.
- Diversifying faculty and having more female faculty can be an important signal for women and increase their confidence.
- Structuring teams in ways that there is greater gender balance can also help.
- There are small daily interactions and ways of communicating within groups that can lead people to have different levels of confidence in their abilities, which need to be addressed.
  
## The Best Communication Advice 

- The best communication advice in five to seven words is "Paint a Picture, Tell a Story."
- If people can put themselves in the communicator's shoes or sets of experiences, it can lead to better communication.
- Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) come from perspective taking and empathy for those who might be different from us.
  
## Communicators to Admire 

- The communicator that Dr. Sterling admires is not a person but instead the linguistic style and ways of communicating in the black church.
- The black church has a rich oral tradition and has been a source of communication for black people throughout history.
  
## Ingredients for Successful Communication 

- The first ingredient for successful communication is to think about the audience's perspective.
- The second ingredient is to focus on the primary message and avoid overloading the audience with too much information.
- The third ingredient is to practice active listening and be responsive to feedback.
## Importance of communication 
- Communication is essential in teaching and conveying information effectively.
- Effective communication requires connecting with the audience emotionally.

## Use of emotion in communication 
- Using emotion in communication can make it more effective.
- It is better to use emotion rather than shy away from it.

## Less is more 
- It is better to keep communication concise and to the point.
- Sometimes, saying less can be more effective.

## Importance of audience 
- Connecting with the audience is essential in effective communication.
- It is important to understand the audience's needs and tailor communication accordingly.

## Teaching vs. communicating 
- Effective instructors understand the difference between merely teaching and effectively communicating.
- Communication requires connecting with the audience on an emotional level.

## Conclusion 
- Effective communication requires connecting with the audience emotionally and understanding their needs.
- Using emotion in communication and keeping communication concise can make it more effective.
- Effective instructors understand the difference between teaching and communicating effectively.

- Scientists played a text-based game with GPT-4 where AI can navigate through a map.

- An AI called TikZ can create beautiful images from a text description.

- GPT-4 AI has never seen an image in its life.

- GPT-4 has impressive mathematical skills.

- Microsoft claims that GPT-4 might have a spark of general intelligence.

# The REAL potential of generative AI

## Large language models 
- Large language models such as GPT are capable of answering questions, writing stories, and engaging in conversation.
- To build a business using this technology, it is important to customize the model to your use case and make it better than what's out there.
- Raza Habib's company, Human Loop, enables large language models to have even greater superpowers.
- Applications and products can be built on top of these models, and the range of use cases is now limited by imagination rather than technology.

## Customizing large language models 
- To customize a large language model, it is important to ask yourself how you can make it really good for your user.
- Human Loop can help you build differentiated applications and products on top of these models.
- The model can be trained on your company's unique data, allowing you to replicate your exact writing style and customized tone.
- Fact-checking answers is also possible, ensuring that the model is safe and reliable.

## Fine-tuning 
- Fine-tuning a model means gathering examples of the outputs you want for the tasks you're trying to do.
- A little bit of extra training is then done on top of the base model to specialize it for that task.
- Fine-tuning is what made the most recent openai text DaVinci 3 model so good that a million users signed up in five days.
- It is also possible to fine-tune the model using something called reinforcement learning from human feedback.

## Challenges with pre-trained models 
- One of the biggest challenges with pre-trained models is that they have a tendency to confidently or hallucinate stuff.
- Sometimes the model is so good that people cannot believe it, but other times it is horrendously wrong.
- The model is originally trained to do expert prediction, so it doesn't necessarily know that it shouldn't be dishonest.
- Human Loop can help reduce hallucinations by making it easy to pull in factual context to the prompt that you give to the model.

## The impact of generative AI on developers 
- Developers are finding that a significant fraction of their code is being written by a large language model.
- The future of large language models might bring societal consequences on the path to AGI.
- It is an ethical minefield, so we need to tread very carefully.

## Basics of large language models 
- Language models are a statistical model of words in the English language.
- They try to predict what the word that'll come next given a few previous words.
- As the language models scale in parameters and the size of the data set they're trained on, they continue to get better.
- They can eventually start doing things like having world knowledge, which allows them to finish sentences like "Today President of the United States acts."

## Differences between large language models 
- The difference between models like GPT and DaVinci 3 is fine-tuning.
- Fine-tuning involves gathering examples of the outputs you want for the tasks you're trying to do and then doing a little bit of extra training on top of the base model to specialize it for that task.
- DaVinci 3 was fine-tuned to specialize it for the tasks that it needed to perform.
## Fine-tuning and reinforcement learning 
- Generative AI models can be fine-tuned using a corpus of books or a company's chat logs or tone of voice from marketing communications.
- Reinforcement learning from human feedback also makes a huge difference to performance.
- The instruct GPT paper that OpenAI released compared a one or two billion parameter model with instruction tuning and RHF to the full GPT-3 model, and people preferred that despite it being a hundred times smaller.
- Anthropics had a paper where they were able to get similar results to RHF without the H, just by having a second model provide the evaluation feedback.

## Fine-tuning data for generative AI models 
- Fine-tuning data can come from two types of data: 
  - Corpus of books, chat logs, tone of voice from marketing communications, or all the emails they've sent.
  - Production usage, capturing the data that customers provide, feedback data, and capturing the edited text and response.

## Problems developers face building generative AI apps 
- Developers face three main problems: prototyping, evaluation, and customization.
- Prototyping involves getting a good prompt that works well for their use case, which tends to be highly iterative.
- Evaluation is harder since the use cases that people are building now tend to be a lot more subjective than you might have done with machine learning before.
- Customization is needed to build something differentiated and for this, developers need to find a way to customize the model to their use case and end-users, and it can be made easier through fine-tuning and a framework for running experiments.

## How generative AI technology will change developer roles 
- In the short-term, generative AI technology augments developers and allows them to do the same thing they could faster.
- GitHub co-pilot is the most impressive application of the large language model so far, which cracked a really novel UX and figured out how to apply a large language model in a way that's now used by 100 million developers.
- On a longer time horizon, developers could become more like product managers in that they're writing the spec, writing documentation, but more of the grunt work and more of the boilerplate is taken care of by models.
## Developers will see their jobs automated 
- As we move towards AGI, developers may be one of the first jobs to see large fractions of their job be automated.
- This is counter-intuitive, but as AI capabilities increase, developers may find their jobs entirely automated.

## Breakthroughs in LLM technology 
- The roadmap for breakthroughs in LLM technology is quite well known.
- There are several things that are coming that we are kind of baked in.
- One thing that developers will really care about is the context window.
- Extending that context window is going to add a lot more capabilities.

## Augmenting large language models 
- One thing that the speaker is very excited about is augmenting large language models with the ability to take actions.
- There are a few examples of this, such as a startup called Adept AI, where the large language model can output a string that says to search the internet for something, and then generate more based on the results.
- This allows you to start treating these large language models much more like agents than just text generation machines.

## AI taking actions 
- AI taking actions is something we have to look forward to, but can this technology just fundamentally be steered in a safe and ethical direction?
- As the capabilities of AI increase, it becomes more pressing to ensure that it is steered in a safe and ethical direction.
- There are a lot of different angles to consider, such as end safety and the risks of AI becoming an existential threat.
- There are also shorter-term threats of social disruption as people feel threatened by these models, as well as ethical questions related to the biases and preferences that were in the model and the data and team that built it at the time that it was being constructed.

## Network effect and replicating GPT3 
- The barriers to entry of training one of these models are mostly capital and talent.

- OpenAI's mission is to build AGI, so that machines can be at the cognitive level of humans if not better.
- Compared to most people's perception in the public, people think it's plausible sooner than a lot of us thought.
- There are prediction markets on this, and the median estimate is something like 2040.
- That's remarkably soon for a technology that might upend almost all of society.
- It is very clear that we are still going to see very dramatic improvements in the short term and even before AGI.
- A lot of societal transformation and economic benefit is expected, but there are also questions that we're going to have to wrestle with to ensure that this is a positive for society.
## The potential of AI and its impact on startups 
- The speaker believes that by 2030, it's plausible that machines can do all the cognitive tasks humans can do and more.
- The range of use cases is now more limited by imagination than by technology.
- When there is a technology change, there are opportunities for new applications, and we're beginning to see that in a Cambrian explosion of new startups.
- At Human Loop, they get a lot of inbound interest from companies that are at the beginning of their explorations and trying to figure out how to take raw models and raw intelligence and turn them into a differentiated product.
- The latest Y Combinator batch has many more startups.

- The speaker is asked if he's building his company in a way that makes sense in a world where machines can do all cognitive tasks humans can do and more.
- He's trying, but it's really hard to internalize that intuitively.
- Stuart Russell has a point where he says that if he told an alien civilization that was going to land on Earth in 50 years, you wouldn't do nothing. There's some possibility that we've got something like an alien arriving soon.
- The speaker feels that it's unbelievably exciting and really difficult to articulate what this new technology means for startups.

## Opportunities for AI engineers 
- Human Loop is hiring and hoping to build a platform that's potentially one of the most disruptive technologies we've ever had and that will ideally be used by millions of developers in the future.
- There's going to be a lot of doing stuff for the first time and inventing novel UX or UI experiences.
- Full-stack developers who are comfortable up and down the stack and deeply care about the end-user experience are ideal candidates.
- They're looking for people who enjoy speaking to their customers, and who are fun to work with because they're working in startups and AI companies that are really on the cutting edge.

## Conclusion

# What Is Ansible? | How Ansible Works? | Ansible Playbook Tutorial For Beginners | DevOps|Simplilearn

## Why use Ansible? 
- Ansible is a tool to help manage services, falling on the operations side of DevOps.
- With increasing numbers of servers, it becomes difficult to create consistent setups.
- Ansible uses code to automate IT setup, which can be repeated and deployed consistently into multiple areas.
- The three key areas that Ansible controls are automation, configuration, and deployment.

## Types of configurations 
- Two different ways of setting up different environments for server farms: pull configuration and push configuration.
- Pull configuration has a master server where instructions are put and a client installed on each server that communicates with the master server.
- Push configuration has no client installed on the remote servers; instructions are pushed out to the servers and force a restructure or fresh clean installation in that environment.
- Ansible is a push configuration server, which contrasts with other popular products like Chef and Puppet.

## Architecture of Ansible 
- When setting up an Ansible environment, the first thing to do is to have a local machine.
- The local machine is where all of the instructions and control are pushed out to the remote server.
- Connected from the local machine are all the different nodes pushing out different configurations that are set up on the local machine.
- The local machine is also the place where you would write configurations in code within a module.
- Each of these modules is actually consistent playbooks.
- The local machine also manages the inventory of nodes that you have in your environment.
- The local machine connects each of the different nodes to your hardware network through ssh clients.
## Ansible Playbooks 

- Ansible's core is playbook
- Playbook is a set of instructions that configure the different nodes in the environment
- Each instruction is written in a language called YAML
- YAML is a standard language used for configuring server environments
- Playbook is designed to make it easy for operations lead to configure the environments that they want to consistently create

## YAML Script 

- YAML script starts with three dashes to indicate the start of a script
- Consists of two distinct plays
- Within each play, nodes are defined
- Specific tasks are then defined for each server environment
- Examples of tasks include installing Apache, starting Tiles, and installing MySQL

## Inventory Management 

- Inventory management is the second part of working with Ansible
- It is where the structure of the network environment is maintained
- Web server and database are examples of nodes created in the inventory
- Each server environment has specific instructions executed on them from the YAML script

## Ansible in the Real World 

- Ansible software is installed on a local machine
- It connects to different nodes within the network
- A playbook is created for how to set up the remote nodes
- An inventory is created to identify how to connect those nodes
- Secure SSH connections are used to encrypt the communication to the servers
- Basic facts on each server are gathered
- The end goal is to have an environment that is consistent

## Ansible Tower 

- Ansible Tower is a framework that was designed to access Ansible
- It is an easy-to-use GUI that makes it easy for non-developers to create the environment they want to manage in their DevOps plan
- Drag and drop mouse click actions are used to create appropriate playbooks, inventories, and pushes for nodes

## Case Study: Hootsuite 

- Hootsuite is a social media management system
- The DevOps team at Hootsuite writes out playbooks that have specific instructions that define the architecture and structure of their hardware nodes and environments
- Ansible has been able to provide Hootsuite with automation, making it easy for them to rebuild and create new servers in a matter of seconds
## Ansible's Key Takeaways 
- Ansible is a product that helps manage a growing network environment.
- Three key areas of success for Ansible are automation, consistent configuration management, and automatic deployment of new software to new or existing servers.
- Ansible can be compared to other popular products such as Chef and Puppet, which provide a similar service.

## Ansible's Architecture 
- Ansible's architecture involves a local machine that pushes out instructions within a playbook managed within modules.
- The inventory is used to manage the actual physical hardware available on the network.

## Setting Up a Physical Ansible Environment 
- Ansible can be set up physically within a network environment.
- Red Hat is developing additional tools for Ansible, including the new Ansible Tower GUI interface, to make it easier to build instructions and playbooks needed to create consistent Ansible environments.

## Use Case: Hootsuite 
- Hootsuite used Ansible to improve the efficiency of their DevOps team.

## Closing 
- Matthew signs off and encourages viewers to subscribe and leave comments about how Ansible compares to Chef and Puppet.

- Tan-Chi starts with the good news in chapter 1 of Romans.
- He mentions that the following week, he will discuss the bad news.
- Tan-Chi explains that starting with the good news prevents discouragement and follows the example of the Apostle Paul.

## Sharing the Good News 
- Tan-Chi emphasizes the importance of sharing the good news.
- He encourages the viewers to share the good news with others.
- Tan-Chi acknowledges the need to know the bad news before sharing the good news.

## Reading Romans Chapter 1 
- The viewers are invited to read Romans chapter 1 together.
- Tan-Chi highlights that Paul describes himself as a bond servant of Christ Jesus and an apostle set apart for the gospel of God.

## Five Things about the Gospel of God 
- Tan-Chi shares five things about the gospel of God found in Romans chapter 1 (more can be discovered in the chapter).
1. The gospel of God is about Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was declared with power through his resurrection from the dead.
2. Through Jesus Christ, we receive grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name.
3. The gospel of God is for all nations, including the Roman Christians.
4. The gospel is powerful and brings salvation to everyone who believes.
5. The gospel reveals the righteousness of God from faith to faith.

## Conclusion 
- Tan-Chi concludes the session by highlighting the five things about the gospel of God.
- He encourages the viewers to continue reading and studying the book of Romans.
## The meaning of the word "gospel" 

- The word "gospel" comes from the Greek word "evangelion."
- "Evangelion" is a combination of two Greek words: "eu" meaning good, and "angelion" meaning proclamation.
- Therefore, the word "gospel" simply means to proclaim good news.

## The origin and authentication of the gospel 

- The gospel is not something that originated from men, but from God Himself. It is called the "gospel of God."
- Our Heavenly Father wants us to know that the good news came from Him. He longs for His lost children and initiated the giving of the good news.
- The gospel is authenticated in the Old Testament by the prophets through their prophecies recorded in the Holy Scriptures.
- The gospel was not invented by the apostles or recently thought of. It has been part of God's plan for a long time.

## The centrality of Jesus in the gospel 

- The gospel is centered on Jesus, the Son of God and a descendant of David according to the flesh.
- The proof of Jesus being the Son of God is His resurrection from the dead by the Spirit of Holiness.
- Understanding that the gospel is about Jesus is crucial because it has the power to change our lives.

## CPR: Three C's, Power, and Righteousness 

- The message of the gospel can be summarized using the acronym CPR: Comes from God, Christ-centered, Compelling, Power to change, and Righteousness of God revealed.
- CPR represents the life-giving power of the gospel to revive spiritually dead people.
- The gospel is not a human invention but originated from God Himself.
- It is centered on Jesus and His redemptive work.
- The gospel is compelling and has the power to transform lives.
- It is the power of God to save and reveals the righteousness of God.

## The definition of the gospel according to Paul 

- In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul defines the gospel as the good news of what Christ has done for us.
- The gospel includes the death of Christ for our sins, His burial, and His resurrection according to the Scriptures.
- Jesus appeared to many people after His resurrection, providing proof that He is the Messiah, the Son of God.

## The age-old promise of the gospel 

- The gospel is not a new concept; it has its roots in the book of Genesis.
- God made a promise to Abraham that through him, all the families of the earth would be blessed.
- This promise was fulfilled through Jesus, the descendant of Abraham, who blesses the entire world.

## The gospel's divine origin 

- The gospel was not invented by men but was preached beforehand by God to Abraham.
- It was part of God's plan to justify the Gentiles by faith and bless all nations through Jesus.

Note: These notes cover Part 2 of the video. Please refer to the other batches for complete notes on the entire video.
## The Gospel in the Old and New Testament 

- The Old Testament gives hints about the coming Messiah, while the New Testament reveals the Gospel clearly.
- In 2 Samuel 7, God promised David that one of his descendants would establish an eternal kingdom.
- The prophet Isaiah also spoke about a child who would be born, a son who would bring peace and establish an everlasting kingdom.

## Understanding the Gospel through the New Testament 

- The Old Testament prophecies can be fully understood when we read the New Testament.
- Daniel's book describes a figure like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, to whom dominion and an everlasting kingdom are given.
- These prophecies ultimately refer to Jesus.

## The Gospel Revealed in Prophecy 

- Prophecies in the Old Testament, such as Isaiah 53, foretell the crucifixion and suffering of the Messiah.
- These prophecies were written in Greek 300 years before Christ, and they align with the New Testament accounts.
- Isaiah 53 describes how the Messiah was pierced for our sins, crushed for our iniquities, and by his scourging, we are healed.

## The Gospel Confirmed by Historical Facts 

- The Gospel is not just a product of human imagination but is confirmed by historical facts.
- Jesus died and rose again, fulfilling the prophecies and establishing his identity as the Son of David.
- The genealogical records in the New Testament confirm that Jesus is the rightful heir to the throne of David.

## The Gospel Compels Obedience 

- The Gospel not only brings grace but also compels obedience.
- Paul, the writer of Romans, experienced the transforming power of the Gospel in his own life.
- The true Gospel will compel believers to live in obedience to God's will.

Note: This is only a partial summary of the video.
## Obedience to the Gospel 
- The importance of obeying the gospel of Jesus
- If someone claims to be a follower of Jesus but refuses to obey His teachings, there is something wrong with their understanding of the gospel
- Refusing to obey is a sign of a fake or counterfeit gospel
- The gospel is authenticated in the Old Testament and centers around Jesus

## Sincere Heart for Obedience 
- The speaker questions if the audience has a sincere heart to obey the gospel
- Highlights the phrase "the obedience of faith" as a reminder of the importance of obedience

## Believers as Saints 
- The audience is referred to as "beloved of God" and "saints"
- The concept of being a saint is different in the Bible compared to popular belief
- In the Bible, believers are considered saints once they come to Jesus and have their sins paid for and washed away

## Acting Like a Saint 
- The speaker encourages the audience to live and act like saints
- Reminds them to identify themselves as saints when looking in the mirror each morning
- Emphasizes that believers are saints who may occasionally sin, but they are no longer sinners who continue to sin

## Paul's Love for the Romans 
- Paul expresses his love and longing to see the believers in Rome
- He mentions how he constantly prays for them and desires to bless them
- Encourages the audience to show love by praying for others

## Paul's Desire to Visit Rome 
- Paul expresses his desire to visit the church in Rome
- This was a unique church that Paul had not planted himself, but he still had a heart for them
- He mentions that he had been prevented from visiting so far, but he still wanted to make Rome a preaching base for the gospel

## Paul's Obligation to Share the Gospel 
- Paul states that he is under obligation to share the gospel with both Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish
- He feels compelled to share the gospel and obtain fruit among the believers in Rome and the rest of the Gentiles
## Understanding Obligation and Debt 
- Paul talks about being in debt and obligated.
- He explains that the English translation of "in debt" is sometimes "under obligation."

## Borrowing Money and Becoming Obligated 
- Paul asks how one gets in debt and becomes obligated.
- He mentions working with banks.
- He clarifies that borrowers are not bankers.

## Entrusting Money and Becoming Obligated 
- Paul gives a demonstration with money.
- He entrusts money to someone and asks if they become obligated.
- He explains that when something is entrusted to someone, they become obligated.

## The Obligation of Sharing the Gospel 
- Paul says that God has entrusted him with the gospel.
- He feels obligated to pass it on.
- He emphasizes that true followers of Jesus are obligated to share the gospel.

## Obligation to Share a Cure 
- Paul asks the audience to think about being obligated assuming they discovered a cure.
- He questions if they would feel obligated to share it with others.

## Obligation and the Power of the Gospel 
- Paul expresses his obligation to Greeks, intellectuals, barbarians, and people from all walks of life.
- He attributes this to understanding the gospel and feeling indebted.
- He says he is eager to share the gospel.

## Not Ashamed of the Gospel 
- Paul declares that he is not ashamed of the gospel.
- He shares his personal experience of initially feeling ashamed to carry a Bible in public.
- As he learned more about the gospel, he realized he had nothing to be ashamed of.

## The Power of the Gospel 
- Paul explains that the gospel is the power of God.
- He compares it to dynamite, emphasizing its ability to change hearts.

## Salvation Through Belief 
- Paul states that the gospel is the power of God for salvation.
- He highlights that salvation is for everyone who believes.

## The Wrath of God 
- Paul mentions that salvation saves us from the penalty of sin and the wrath of God.
- He teases that the topic of the wrath of God will be discussed in the next week's session.
## Understanding the Wrath of God 

- The wrath of God and the righteousness of God do not conflict.
- It is important to understand the wrath of God in order to take the gospel message seriously.

## The Power of God to Transform Lives 

- God wants to save us from the power of sin and give us victory over our struggles.
- Whether it's addiction, selfishness, or any other problem, God is working to transform us through a process called sanctification.
- As believers, we are being transformed to be like Christ.

## The Righteousness of God Revealed 

- The Bible tells us that the gospel reveals the righteousness of God.
- The gospel is the power of God that saves us and shows us God's righteousness.

## The Meaning of the Righteousness of God 

- The righteousness of God is not just about God's character and actions.
- It also includes how God forgives us and saves us.
- Justice and love meet at the cross, where Jesus paid the penalty for our sins.
- The righteousness of God means that our sins are forgiven and we are declared righteous.

## Two Kinds of Righteousness 

- There are two kinds of righteousness mentioned by Paul in Philippians 3.
- The first kind is a righteousness that comes from human effort and obedience to the law, but it is not enough to bring us to heaven.
- The second kind is the righteousness that comes from God through faith in Jesus.
- When we come to Jesus, God sees us through the righteousness of Christ.

## The Amazing Gospel of God 

- The gospel of God is amazing because it comes from Him and is centered on Jesus.
- It has the power to change us and make us alive spiritually.
- It is about the righteousness of God in us.

## The Christian Life Begins and Ends with Faith 

- The Christian life begins and continues by faith.
- The righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith.
- Faith is essential in the Christian life from start to finish.

Note: This is a partial batch of notes, continue with the next batch for complete coverage of the video.
## Faith in Christ
 Many people think I received Jesus Christ by faith, and now I sustain my Christian life by works, but that is not true. From beginning to end, it's all about faith. I begin my relationship with God by faith, and I will sustain my relationship with God by faith.

## The Book of Romans
 The book of Romans teaches us that faith is the evidence of our salvation. Faith without works is dead. It is through faith that we are saved, not by our own efforts or works. It is a gift from God, and it is not something we can boast about.

## The Gospel of God
 The gospel of God is all about the good news. There are four key elements of the gospel: 
- It comes from God
- It is Christ-centered
- It compels us to change
- It compels us to share

## The Power of the Gospel
 Paul says that he is not ashamed of the gospel because there is power in it. The gospel has the power to save us. It is the righteousness of God revealed through faith.

## Faith in the Gospel
 Faith is simply acknowledging that we cannot save ourselves and trusting in the promises of God. We surrender our lives to Jesus and place our faith in Him. Faith is the key to our relationship with God.

## Religion vs. the Gospel
 There is a difference between religion and the gospel. Religion is man's way to find God through much effort and by earning salvation through works. On the other hand, the gospel is God's way to find us. It is salvation by grace, not by our own efforts. It is a gift that we don't deserve.

## Assurance of Salvation
 Religion will never assure us of salvation, but the gospel gives us assurance of heaven. The gospel is all about the good news of what Jesus has done for us.

## Accepting the Gospel
 If you have been touched by the gospel of God and you want to accept it, you can pray to receive Jesus Christ as your Lord and Savior by faith. Admit that you are a sinner, believe that Jesus died on the cross to pay for your sins, and invite Him into your life.

## Public Confession
 Making a public confession of our faith is important. It shows that we are not ashamed of Jesus and that we are committed to following Him. By standing up and publicly declaring our faith, we affirm our commitment to Jesus.

## Salvation by Faith
 Salvation is given not by mental belief, but when we ask for it by faith. It is not about our own efforts or works, but about trusting in Jesus and His sacrifice on the cross.


## Sharing the Good News 

- Peter Tan-Chi emphasizes the importance of making a stand for God.
- Believers are encouraged to help others grow in their faith.
- One way to do this is by learning to follow God every day.
- Another way is by studying the Bible and seeking its guidance.
- Above all, believers should rest in what God has done for them, rather than trying to impress Him.

## Doing Things Out of Love 

- Peter Tan-Chi acknowledges that believers cannot do anything to impress God.
- Instead, their actions should come from a place of love for Him.
- Believers should strive to love God in all aspects of their life, including worship and studying the Bible.
- This love should be reciprocated, as God loves His people.

## Living a Life of Love 

- The ultimate goal for believers is to live a life of love.
- This love should result in a life of holiness.
- By living in love and holiness, believers can experience the abundant life that Jesus offers.
- Peter Tan-Chi concludes the segment with a prayer, asking God to help believers live a life of love.

## Conclusion and Blessing 

- Peter Tan-Chi ends the segment by praying for God's blessing upon the audience.
- He also thanks the viewers for joining him and concludes with "God bless you guys."

## L'avenir de l'Ukraine une fois la guerre terminée 
- Une fois la guerre terminée, l'Ukraine sera endettée à l'égard de l'Occident, sans même parler des coûts de reconstruction estimés à 800 milliards. 
- Certains craignent que le pays devienne une colonie souveraine sur papier, mais financièrement captive de l'Occident pour les décennies à venir. 



## Une nouvelle méthode pour éviter le scénario catastrophe 
- Il est encore possible d'éviter le scénario catastrophe en déployant une nouvelle méthode spectaculairement controversée et potentiellement dangereuse.


## Contexte
- L'économie ukrainienne est essentiellement au bord du précipice, avec un PIB effondré et deux fois plus d'inflation et de taux d'intérêt que la moyenne.
- Le gouvernement ukrainien peine à payer les salaires et doit emprunter toujours plus d'argent, et il est estimé qu'en 2023 il aura besoin de 3 milliards de dollars par mois.
- La Banque mondiale estime que l'économie ukrainienne s'est contractée d'environ 35 % en 2022, comparativement à une baisse de seulement 4 ou 5% pour l'économie russe.



## Contributions Occidentales
- Les États-Unis, l'Union européenne et leurs alliés ont accepté de financer presque l'entièreté des besoins de l'Ukraine, en injectant des dizaines de milliards de dollars et d'euros en argent, équipements, munitions et contributions.
- La contribution totale des États-Unis dépasse maintenant l'entièreté du budget militaire de la Russie.
- La plupart des contributions de l'Occident sont facturées au gouvernement ukrainien, et le financement international de l'Ukraine atteint environ 100 milliards de dollars, dont 18% sous forme de dons et 82% sous forme de prêts remboursables avec intérêt.



## Programme de Prêts Buy-Oulanis
- Les États-Unis ont annoncé le retour du programme de prêts Buy-Oulanis, une initiative controversée créée par Winston Churchill pendant la Deuxième Guerre mondiale. 
- Le programme permet d'accélérer le transfert des armes et d'accumuler rapidement une dette spectaculaire envers les États-Unis.
- Une fois la guerre terminée, les États-Unis et l'Ukraine s'entendront sur une dette qui risque de représenter seulement une fraction de l'assistance offerte.


## Impacts économiques de la guerre en Ukraine
- La dette américaine et les prétentions de la Chine et de la Russie ne sont pas complètement fausses. L'Ukraine devra bel et bien rembourser les États-Unis et ce pour les décennies à venir. 
- Il existe des questions très sérieuses quant à la capacité de l'Ukraine à rembourser cette dette un jour, car elle est le pays le plus pauvre de toute l'Europe. 
- Le modèle économique de l'Ukraine est largement basé sur la conversion des ressources naturelles et de l'énergie afin de produire des produits industriels destinés à l'exportation via la mer Noire. 
- Ce modèle est lourdement dépendant des intrantes d'énergie et de ressources naturelles, en particulier en provenance de Russie. 
- La grande majorité de la richesse industrielle et des régions les plus économiquement productives sont concentrées au Sud et à l'Est, exactement dans les territoires revendiqués par la Russie. 
- L'Ukraine a toujours servi d'État transit pour la Russie afin de livrer du gaz naturel en Europe, mais cette source de revenus est maintenant perdue pour toujours. 
- En raison des réfugiés et des pertes humaines, des territoires perdus et d'un taux de natalité parmi les plus bas de toute la planète, l'Ukraine estime qu'elle pourrait se retrouver à l'issue de la guerre avec seulement 28 millions d'habitants.



## Responsabilité de l'Occident pour la dette ukrainienne
- Certains soutiennent que la dette envers les pays occidentaux devrait être entièrement pardonnée, car le conflit contre la Russie dépasse largement les intérêts de l'Ukraine. 
- On pourrait argumenter que l'armée ukrainienne agit essentiellement comme une extension des intérêts occidentaux qui lui ont fourni de l'argent et des ressources volontiers. 
- Sans parler de dette, il faut souligner que l'Ukraine n'a presque plus d'argent et a des dettes à une vitesse pharaonique, même pour rester en vie. 
- Après la guerre, le pays devra rembourser une dette stratosphérique malgré la destruction de son infrastructure, la perte de territoire et de ressources hautement stratégiques, la réduction massive du nombre de contribuables et l'effondrement prévisible de son modèle économique.


## Consequences of a debt-funded reconstruction
- If the war ends and the inflation stabilizes, it is estimated that the reconstruction of Ukraine could cost anywhere from 500 to 800 billion dollars. 
- The Ukrainian budget before the war was only 40 billion dollars, equivalent to the state of Maryland in the US. 
- Ukraine will have to take out massive loans to pay for the reconstruction, but the question remains who will lend the money and at what price? 
- A survey conducted in 28 developed countries revealed that due to the current economic climate, two-thirds of respondents did not think their country should provide financial assistance to Ukraine. 
- Russia is unlikely to pay the entire bill for the damage caused by the war, and other countries are unlikely to donate their own resources. 
- In order to secure funding, the Occident may have to resort to "strong measures" - such as freezing Russian bank accounts and seizing the funds - to pay for Ukraine’s reconstruction. 
- However, this poses a number of risks and dangers, both financial and geopolitical. 
- Such a decision would lack legitimacy due to the International Criminal Court’s lack of authority over states and Russia not being a member. 
- A resolution of this kind is unlikely to pass in the UN due to several of Russia’s allies and neutral countries being afraid of setting a precedent and having their own reserves seized one day. 
- Such an action would also have serious consequences, as history has taught us that badly negotiated or perceived as unfair peace treaties can lead directly to wars.


## Consequences de la Première Guerre mondiale sur l'Allemagne
- Le traité de Versailles a forcé l'Allemagne à payer des réparations gigantesques, ce qui a poussé le pays vers la catastrophe économique et mis la table pour la montée du régime mittentérien et l'éclatement de la Deuxième guerre mondiale.



## Risques encourus par l'Occident
- Il y a un risque bien réel que l'Occident tente de pousser trop loin son privilège en saisissant les réserves de la Russie. La population russe resterait profondément hostile et rancunière envers l'Occident, ouvrant la porte à des leaders beaucoup plus enclins à utiliser la violence que Vladimir Poutine. Sans rien à perdre, cela pourrait précipiter une nouvelle invasion de l'Ukraine ou pire, un conflit direct.



## Est-ce une arnaque?
- Il faut reconnaître qu'il y a quelque chose d'hypocrite à prétendre que la lutte contre la Russie est strictement le combat de l'Ukraine et que l'Occident n'a aucune responsabilité dans les circonstances qui contribuent à créer et à perpétuer le conflit. Les grands gagnants sont sans équivoque les États-Unis; victoire ou défaite, ils sont garantis d'être remboursés avec intérêt et ce jusqu'au dernier dollar.



## Conséquences sur l'Ukraine
- Difficile de faire des prédictions quant à l'avenir de l'Ukraine, mais l'écrasante majorité de la dette et de la facture reconstruction devrait être remboursée non pas par la Russie mais par l'Ukraine elle-même. C'est une question stratégique pour les États-Unis et l'Ukraine devra se plier aux volontés de la Banque Mondiale, du FMI et de l'Union Européenne.


## Impact du FMI et de la Banque mondiale
- L'intervention du FMI et de la Banque Mondiale en Ukraine place le remboursement des dettes comme la priorité numéro un, malgré les conséquences néfastes sur les citoyens ukrainiens.
- En 2022, l'Ukraine a remboursé près de 560 millions de dollars à la Banque Mondiale, incluant 150 millions en frais de délinquance.



## Impact de l'aide de l'Occident
- Mon objectif n'est pas de suggérer que l'Ukraine n'aurait jamais dû accepter l'aide de l'Occident, mais de mettre en avant la réalité et de briser l'illusion de solidarité.
- En effet, l'Ukraine devra payer pour cette générosité et cela sera clair une fois que la guerre sera terminée.



## Exploitation par les grandes puissances
- L'Ukraine n'est qu'un vulgaire pion dans la partie d'échecs entre les grandes puissances et la guerre profite avant tout à ceux qui la finance.
- Les intérêts stratégiques de douzaines de pays développés n'entrent pas en compte et les promesses ne seront jamais tenues. L'Ukraine ne sera pas admise au sein de l'OTAN ou de l'Union Européenne dans un avenir proche.

# You should create things for a billion people, not just tech giant monopolies

## Apple's control of our devices [00:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h00m03s)
- Apple has a stranglehold on our devices, preventing us from communicating with our friends with different devices. 
- This is due to Apple's desire to maintain a monopoly. 
- The problem is that messages sent from an Android device to an iPhone device don't show up on the other device. 

## US Bills [01:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h01m15s)
- A pair of new bills are hitting the US Congress that require our help in order to get passed. 
- These bills will give us more freedom and break down Apple's walled garden. 
- It will also create more competition and satisfy more customers. 

## Technological Optimism [01:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h01m40s)
- Corey Doctorow believes that self-determination is about having the final say over how we live our lives and not about superficial desires for different colors or moving desktop menu icons. 
- It's possible to be a technological optimist but still not want tech giants to control everything. 
- Working at these places stifles innovation by default, as the decisions and outcomes are not driven by the people at the bottom of the totem pole.

## Scaling the Size of the Company [02:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h02m33s)
- Paul Graham suggests that we can adjust the amount of freedom we have by scaling the size of the company we work for. 
- If you start the company, you'll have the most freedom, and even a company with 100 people will feel different than one with a thousand. 

## Lock-in Network Effects [03:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h03m53s)
- Beeper co-founder Eric Miguelski explains that the lock-in network effects prevent new competitors with innovative ideas from getting off the ground. 
- Most users don't use these apps because of specific features, they use them because their friends are on the app. 
- We don't want big tech to have this much power, but they are designed to in a lot of ways. 

## Apple's Motivation [05:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h05m01s)
- Craig Federighi's deposition explains why Apple wouldn't bring iMessage to Android - it would remove an obstacle to iPhone families giving their kids Android phones. 
- Apple's motivation is about money and lock-in - it's their moat.
## Problem [05:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h05m19s)
- The biggest technology companies today, such as Amazon, Apple, Facebook, and Google, can use manipulative tactics to steer users away from rival services and even kill competition.
- These tech giants also stifle user freedom by making it practically impossible to switch networks, such as when WhatsApp changed its privacy policy earlier this year.

## Solution [05:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h05m42s)

# Reid Hoffman and Sam Altman | AI Field Notes

## Overview (0:00)
- This is a Greylock podcast where they share stories from company builders and business leaders.
- In this episode, Greylock General Partner Reid Hoffman talks with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman about Hoffman's new book that he co-wrote with GPT-4, which is OpenAI's most advanced language model to date.

## AI Advancements (1:00)
- The past year has been marked by launch after launch of groundbreaking AI products.
- OpenAI's early regenerative text tools GPT-3 and chatbot GBT, and the text to image generator DALL-E.

- The internet has been buzzing with a proliferation of AI-generated images, so realistic they became "deep fakes."

## Impromptuteeeeeee Book (5:00)
- Keeping up with all the AI advancements and their immediate impact is why Hoffman wrote "Impromptu."
- The book is intended to act as a travelogue of his experience with GPT-4.
- Above all, Hoffman sees AI as a human amplifier but urges it must be developed safely.
- Safety is exactly what OpenAI is striving for, according to Altman.
- Hoffman's detailed chronicle of experience with GPT-4 is exactly the kind of data the organization needs to continue developing the technology with safety in mind.

- Hoffman's book is about amplification intelligence or augmentation intelligence versus artificial intelligence.
- Amplifying human ability is the primary goal.
- GPT-4 is a collaborator and co-pilot to work with.
